## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet, and the starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds. The default recipe gives only about 32 PPO updates (131k steps at 4096 steps per update). The likeliest bottleneck is too few samples and updates, not the network's capacity. Cutting ppo_epochs buys more environment samples within the same compute. The task also has a clear structure: a brick is correct when every footprint cell, at the layer where the brick lands (the highest filled cell under the footprint plus one), is a missing target cell. A network that keeps per-layer features and pools them over each footprint layer by layer should learn this more easily than one that mixes all layers together at the first 1x1 convolution. This round: two recipe-only changes on the starting network (2 epochs and 1 epoch), plus one per-layer architecture trained with the 2-epoch recipe so the architecture's effect can be seen on its own.

### Round 2
All four runs so far, including the starting architecture, scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 in training. That held across 1, 2 and 4 epochs and 139k–401k samples, and across two network designs. So recipe changes alone have not got learning off the floor. Every network tried also shared one built-in assumption: footprint pooling with the anchor at the brick's top-left corner. r1c2 also assumed a layer order. The task warns that the world may not behave as described. If the anchor rule, the footprint orientation or the layer order differs, those heads score the wrong cells and the agent cannot learn. This round drops those assumptions. A learned 3x3 output conv lets each brick type learn its own anchor offset. The legal-action mask goes in as one input plane per brick type, which shows how far each brick reaches near the grid edges. A global context vector feeds the placement and DONE decisions. I test this head with two recipes, plus a cell-attention version.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 in training, across very different trunks (CNN, per-layer CNN, transformer), heads (top-left footprint pooling, learned 3x3 conv) and recipes (1 or 2 epochs, 128 to 512 envs). Seed noise can't explain a floor that complete. Something structural is probably wrong. The likeliest cause is that this world's action-to-cell mapping differs from the stated one, for example transposed axes, a different anchor, or reordered types. Every head so far ties logit position to spatial position, and a local conv head can't learn a transpose or a reordering. So this round tests heads that assume nothing about layout: a fully connected map from features to all placement logits. If any of these scores above 0 while the spatially tied heads stay at 0, that supports the mapping explanation. If they also score 0, the problem is more likely in the dynamics or reward, not the head.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 on train success. That held across very different heads (footprint pooling, layer-wise, attention, dense, pure MLP), across 1, 2 and 4 epochs, and from 140k to 410k samples. Since no head mattered, the action layout and the network's capacity are unlikely causes. The likelier cause is the training dynamics, which were only ever run near the default reward settings (gamma 0.95, entropy 0.01). Under a random policy most placements land outside the target and earn negative reward, while DONE earns 0. The policy may therefore learn to quit early before it learns where to place bricks. The per-step reward is dense, and choosing the best immediate placement is close to the right policy. So a short-horizon recipe (gamma 0.9, lambda 0.8) with low entropy should give a cleaner, lower-variance signal. This last round tests that recipe on the two most task-shaped networks, plus a separate critic network.
